<reason>A genuine framing battle, well argued on both sides. A (CON) built a strong case that the harm is conditional on cutting instructional time while savings and staffing gains are universal, weaponized B's concession that time-holding districts show "small or near zero" losses, and reframed retention as itself a learning variable — a mechanism B never refuted. But B (PRO) won the decisive ground. First, B forced evaluation of the calendar as actually adopted, and A's only answer to the frequency question was an honest but costly dodge ("I will not invent a precise share"), leaving B's claim that most adopters cut time standing. Second, B's "same dial" argument showed harm and savings covary, so A could not pocket universal savings while quarantining harm in a subset; A's response leaned on stretching the "small or near zero" concession from time-holders to all adopters, and B's closing caught that misattribution cleanly. Third, B's reductio that A's Friday enrichment remedy is "a fifth day rebuilt at small scale" undercut A's escape hatch. A's path (motion fails as written because the failure mode is optional) was live throughout, but B did more to make the debate decidable on the motion's natural empirical reading. Both sides had clipped turns and clean Q/A formatting; neither used fake sourcing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 "you cannot have it both ways" [B4.5] — either most districts hold hours (savings shrink toward nothing) or most cut time (A has conceded the learning loss) — paired with the closing catch [B5.3] that A stretched the "small or near zero" concession from the thin time-holding minority to every adopter. A never repaired that overreach, and it was the load-bearing move of A's case.</best_rebuttal>
